The final Part 1 model (sub_51), step by step

Read it left to right: steps 1–3 build the actuarial model A for every peril; step 4 is a small boosting partner B; step 5 blends them with a fixed weight per line; step 6 multiplies by the policy's own claims experience.

expected cost = [ w × A + (1 − w) × B ] × M
Show the details: what each step is and why
StepWhat it isWhy
Frequency, per perilAdditive Poisson model: a GAM fitted by boosting with one-split trees, so no interactions. Offset log(exposure × completeness) − trend.Beat models with interactions on 14 of 15 perils and a per-peril GLM in 28 of 30 peril-years.
Severity, per perilGamma on a few drivers: log sum insured for the small home perils, a constant for motor bodily injury.Claim sizes barely depend on the rating factors.
Large lossesCapped at 150k / 250k / 50k (motor / buildings / contents) and reloaded on the line per exposure.A handful of very large claims would otherwise drive the fit.
Experience rating MBühlmann–Straub on the policy's own claims: M = (N + k) / (E + k); k = 16 motor, 8 home; subsidence excluded in buildings.The largest single gain (+0.0025).
Boosting partnerLightGBM Tweedie written by the local model, reviewed and corrected before use, trained on the gross target.Adds +0.0003 in the blend.

The final Part 2 model (p2_sub_21), step by step

Two years of new data cannot support a model of their own, so they adjust the Part 1 model instead of replacing it: 1 start from the Part 1 model as prior, 2 rescale it to the emerging cost level, 3 add only the few corrections the new data can support. The rest of this tab shows the evidence for each step.

expected cost = prior × level × corrections

The acquired broker portfolio

What the insurer's own premium knows

The final Part 2 model (p2_sub_21), line by line

Expected cost = prior × emerging level × correction. Prior: the Part 1 frequency × severity model refitted on the developed market with the shared columns (home: the variant with relative premium). Level: per line with credibility; storm at its own level, contents per peril. Correction: motor, the average of two GLMs on the prior (new business, gender, relative premium; the second also fuel and cover type) times a boost on claim counts; contents, gender and working from home; buildings, 10% of an emerging-only model.

LineStepWhat it doesEntered in (bench Δ shape / own ×10⁻⁴, checks won)

From risk premium to the price the customer pays

Part 2 also asks for the office premium of 20 reference policies: the model gives the expected claims cost (risk premium); expenses, reinsurance, commissions, tax and profit turn it into a price. This tab shows that step and how uncertain the price is.

All rates are given by the competition (the expenses table, emerging column). Our choices, with their effect on the total of the 20 policies: the fixed expense is pro-rated by exposure (per policy instead: +2.7%); tax and profit are shares of the office premium (on the risk premium instead: −13.5%); cat reinsurance applies to the property lines only (without it: −3.8%); the comparison-site commission is blank in the emerging market and none of the 20 policies uses that channel.

2–3× today's premium
Claims alone cost 67% (motor), 109% (buildings) and 64% (contents) of today's written premium; with broker loadings the office premium is 2–3 times it (median 2.4).
Main uncertainty: new business
+19% over renewals (CI90 0–41%), driven by five large bodily-injury claims; kept because an acquired portfolio is usually worse.
Other limits
Borrowed trends: ±2 points a year of severity trend = ±3% on the price. Buildings level: about ±16% on two years of fire and storm.
The full table of the 20 policies is in the report appendix; the sensitivity of the total to each assumption is below.

Code map: where everything is in the repository

Data sources (files in docs/dashboard_data/ of the repository)

  • Autonomous AI loops — Outcome of every experiment in the local Qwen research loops, from each loop's results.tsv, Part 1 and Part 2.
  • Independent recomputation — Checks of the 25 Oct independent recomputation of Part 2 by area (results_p2/audit_controlli.csv).
  • Decision register — Every decision: the actuary's instruction or check, or the AI finding, with evidence, rejected alternative, decision, effect and source file (docs/DECISIONS_actuary.md).
  • Errors and challenges — AI errors caught by checks and actuary challenges that became checks, from the project logs.
  • Explanatory text — The paragraphs that explain each tab, written from the project documents and the report.
  • Part 1 submissions — Public and private score of every Part 1 Kaggle submission of the team (Kaggle CLI, after the close).
  • Reporting-delay backtest — Accident year 2023 claims reported by end-2024: predicted with the developed market's delay curve vs actual, per peril (results_p2/audit_backtest_denuncia.csv).
  • Seven-check bench decisions — Every Part 2 idea on the seven-check bench: mean change vs the reference (×0.0001 D²), checks won and verdict (results_p2/p2_bench*.csv).
  • Part 2 final model — The final Part 2 model step by step and line by line, with the submission each step entered in and its bench result.
  • New-business variants — Motor new-business correction: three versions, 2025 motor rate and public Kaggle score.
  • Assumption sensitivity — Change in the 2025 level per line when one assumption changes (results_p2/sensitivity.csv).
  • Part 2 submissions — Every Part 2 submission with its public score, marked as candidate or diagnostic probe. Downloaded with the Kaggle CLI.
  • Prior vs new data only — D² on emerging 2024 of a model fitted on 2023: emerging data only vs Part 1 prior × emerging level (results_p2/p2_compare.csv).
  • Target chain by year — Cost per exposure year by accident year: reported, ultimate and at the 2025 level, per line and market.
  • Claims per row — Share of policy rows with 0, 1, 2 and 3+ claims per line and market.
  • Data cleaning — Every data fix in both markets with its status (applied, tested and not adopted, flagged only), rows affected, evidence and action.
  • Column dictionary — Every raw column with its status (used, rebuilt, key, excluded as leakage, decoy or other), the reason, missing share and number of distinct values.
  • Experience rating factors — The Bühlmann–Straub factor (N + k)/(E + k) over expected claims for 0–3 claims seen, k = 8 and 16.
  • Reporting delay curves — Share of claims reported within N days per peril (reverse-time estimator, developed market).
  • Error decomposition — Share of the Tweedie deviance due to rating factors, history, unseen policy risk and noise (calibrated simulation).
  • Derived features — Features built from the raw columns and why.
  • Judge decisions — Changes read on the three judges (deviance change ×1e-4, 2023 / 2024) and the decision taken; from docs/WORKLOG.md
  • The judges — What each judge scores, what it is good at, its weakness and what it was used for.
  • Large losses — Cap, number of claims above, excess and load per exposure year per line.
  • All Part 1 models — Every model fitted in Part 1 (50 sets of out-of-fold predictions) re-scored on the final target with the three judges, by fold and by line, with the time each was built; from scripts/judge_all_models.py.
  • One-way analysis — Observed and predicted relativities by class for every variable, three models, out-of-fold (results/oneway.json).
  • Broker vs new business test — AUC of a classifier telling the 2025 broker policies from 2023–24 emerging new business on the rating variables (0.5 = indistinguishable).
  • Portfolio composition — Share of exposure by class of each rating variable for five populations (developed, emerging renewals and new business, 2025 renewals, 2025 broker portfolio).
  • Observed frequency and cost — Reported claim frequency, average claim cost and cost per exposure year per peril: developed market, emerging renewals and emerging new business.
  • Broker portfolio profile — Expected cost under the prior and key rating variables for emerging renewals and new business 2023–24 and the two parts of the 2025 book.
  • Perils by market — Claims, frequency, average cost, cost per exposure, reporting delay and open share per peril, developed vs emerging market.
  • Qwen experiments — Every experiment of every local Qwen loop with its outcome, score and best score kept so far, from each loop's results.tsv.
  • What Qwen kept — Every change the Qwen loops kept, in Qwen's words, and what happened to it.
  • Qwen loops and roles — What Qwen could change in each loop, how it was judged and the outcome.
  • Qwen code review — From Qwen's 125 code-review findings to the fixes made, from autoresearch_review.
  • Claim size percentiles — Percentiles of net incurred per claim by line and market.
  • Additive vs interactions — D² per peril of an additive frequency model against one with interactions (fit 2021–23, score 2024), with main drivers.
  • Database tables — Rows, columns, years and grain of every raw table, both markets (aggregates only).
  • Trends per peril — Frequency and severity trends per peril with p-values and the rule applied.
  • Workflow map — Each stage of the actuarial workflow: the actuary's direction, the AI's execution, how it was verified and the evidence file.
